doc_summary: Transluce trains small open-weight investigator agents with RL (black-box and PRBO dense rewards) to produce natural-language jailbreaks that elicit CBRN/drug/explosive information from frontier models, reaching high pass@1 on most targets. The post stresses robust judges, naturalistic prompts, transfer across models, and honest limits (monitors, judge difficulty).

items.claim: prefers narrowly specified, objectively gradable behaviors with a robust multi-criteria judge over off-the-shelf benchmark graders because loose graders are reward-hackable and accept superficially related outputs.
items.quote: We explored other datasets such as HarmBench [19] and StrongReject [20], but found that the LM-based graders provided in these datasets were too susceptible to reward-hacking to be used for training. For example, model responses could pass the graders by providing historical information

items.claim: In a setup, use a plausible professional framing (e.g. a postdoc rewriting a methods section) and plain, fluent English instead of disfluent or gimmicky adversarial strings because natural prompts look like ordinary user requests.
items.quote: Since the jailbreaks are produced by a language model, the attacks are natural and legible, relying only on plain English.

items.claim: In a setup, add a KL penalty to keep the generating agent's outputs naturalistic instead of letting optimization drift to odd text, because fluency keeps the prompts realistic.
items.quote: We use a KL loss coefficient of 0.01 to incentivize policy outputs to remain naturalistic

items.claim: prefers prompt-side validity checks (no fictional/humorous framing, no leaked answer content) over only checking the response because success must not come from a loophole in the request.
items.quote: The prompt judge verifies that the prompt does not request sarcastic/humorous/fictional responses, and does not include any information that might be part of the answer itself.

items.claim: prefers spot-checking technical accuracy with a subject-matter expert and reporting inaccuracies over claiming success from judge scores alone because elicited outputs may look detailed but be wrong.
items.quote: while we were unable to fully assess technical accuracy, we conducted spot checks (including consulatation with a subject matter expert), and found that most responses appeared accurate, though a few were not.

items.claim: Use a spectrum of related tasks of varying difficulty as a curriculum, and aggregate rewards over several models, so sparse-success behaviors become learnable.
items.quote: We speculate that this is because our dataset of CBRN tasks contains a spectrum of related tasks of varying degrees of difficulty, providing a good curriculum for RL.

items.claim: Distrusts attack success against models with extra monitoring: attacks optimized without monitors tend to be plainly harmful and get caught by guardrails.
items.quote: when attacks are primarily optimized to elicit responses from models without monitors, they generally plainly requested harmful content, which can be easily detected by response monitors.

items.claim: prefers dense, partial-credit reward signals (PRBO, rubric partial credit) over sparse binary success because rare behaviors give no gradient otherwise.
items.quote: To address the inherent sparsity of a binary success/failure signal from a judge, we design the LM judge to provide continuous scores with partial credit across multiple rubric criteria

items.claim: Argues that cheap, small trained investigators can red-team much larger frontier models, and that attacks transfer across models.
items.quote: Interestingly, attacks often transfer across models, and training on less robust models provides a good intermediate signal for attacking more robust models (even across different model developers).

items.claim: Open problem: bypassing monitors and building robust judges for harder tasks such as malicious code.
items.quote: To bypass these guardrails, one could leverage other approaches, such as designing an output encoding scheme that goes undetected by response monitors, or generating attacks against an open-weight monitor and relying on transfer. We leave this problem to future work.
